record.question:
An online retailer expects a sharp burst of checkout requests during a sale. Users sign in with Google or Facebook. The checkout service must durably accept orders even when payment and fulfillment workers are temporarily at capacity. The UI may show a pending order and later display the completed result. Repeated requests must not create duplicate orders.

Which design best supports these requirements?

options.text: Use CloudFront and an ALB with an EC2 Auto Scaling group. Authenticate users through Amazon Cognito and complete payment processing synchronously before inserting each order into a Multi-AZ RDS database.
Use CloudFront and an ALB with an EC2 Auto Scaling group and Cognito sign-in. Send orders to SQS using an EC2 role. Scale separate idempotent workers to process orders and persist status in DynamoDB.
Host the frontend on an S3 website endpoint and add that endpoint to Global Accelerator. Use Cognito sign-in and have the browser write completed orders directly to DynamoDB.
Use CloudFront and an ALB with a fixed-size EC2 fleet and Cognito sign-in. Complete each payment request synchronously in the web tier before writing the order to DynamoDB.

explanation.text:
Choose <<2>>. The queue provides a durable boundary between request acceptance and downstream work. Web capacity and worker capacity can scale independently, while order status in DynamoDB supports the pending-to-completed user flow. Use role credentials and enforce authorization before accepting an order.

<<1>> retains a synchronous dependency on payment processing. It cannot durably accept checkout work while those workers are at capacity; adding database redundancy does not create a backlog. <<3>> uses an unsupported Global Accelerator endpoint type; S3 content delivery belongs behind a service such as CloudFront. Writing a record also does not establish that payment and fulfillment succeeded. <<4>> has no durable backlog and couples checkout acceptance to the fixed web fleet and downstream response time. DynamoDB itself is not the scalability defect.

SQS standard queues can deliver a message more than once. Store a stable order or idempotency key and make payment and status transitions safe to retry. A successful enqueue means accepted for processing, not payment completed; report those states accurately to the customer.

AWS documentation (checked September 18, 2026): [SQS standard queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues.html), [Global Accelerator endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/global-accelerator/latest/dg/about-endpoints.html). [Cognito social sign-in](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-social-idp.html).

diagram_alt: Checkout acceptance, processing, retry and completion are separate states, with one order ID across retries.

sources.supports: SQS decouples producers and workers; standard queues can deliver duplicate or out-of-order messages.
Standard accelerator endpoints are ALBs, NLBs, EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses, not S3 website endpoints.
Cognito user pools integrate Facebook and Google sign-in with user pool tokens.

editorial_notes: Introduced asynchronous pending status and idempotency to make the queued checkout behavior correct.
Removed unsupported claims that DynamoDB cannot scale or that RDS is always more expensive.
Strengthened the first distractor to use valid Cognito authentication; its failure is the synchronous processing dependency.
